Since some parts of the mouth and throat are not easy to see when you open your mouth, a health care provider might feel (palpate) your oral cavity and use a special mirror or fiberoptic scope to look at these areas. Dental exam It is important to tell your dentist about your head and neck cancer and to have regular dental cleanings and checkups. Distress screening It is normal to have strong feelings about being diagnosed with cancer and your feelings can also change from day to day and week to week. Talk to your care team and those whom you feel most comfortable about how you are feeling. There are services and people who can help you. Support and counseling are available. Many treatment teams include mind and body therapists who can help. Dealing with a cancer diagnosis can be stressful and may cause further distress. Distress is an unpleasant experience of a mental, physical, social, or spiritual nature. It can affect how you feel, think, and act. Distress might include feelings of sadness, fear, helplessness, worry, anger, and guilt. You may also experience depression, anxiety, and sleep issues. Your treatment team will screen your level of distress. This is part of your cancer care. Your diagnosis of cancer may affect your family or loved ones. They may feel some degree of anxiety or depression. They can talk to the social worker and seek help, too. Therefore, blood tests to look at thyroid endocrine levels might be done before and/or after treatment. An audiogram is a graph showing the results of a pure-tone hearing test. Tumors in the head and neck can affect hearing. Treatment of head and neck tumors can also affect hearing. Your preferences about treatment are always important. Fertility (all genders) Treatment such as chemotherapy can affect your fertility, the ability to have children. If you think you want children in the future, ask your care team how cancer and cancer treatment might change your fertility. To preserve your fertility, you may need to take action before starting cancer treatment. Those who want to have children in the future should be referred to a fertility specialist to discuss the options before starting treatment. Fertility preservation is all about keeping your options open, whether you know you want to have children later in life or aren’t really sure at the moment. Fertility and reproductive specialists can help you sort through what may be best for your situation. More information on fertility preservation in adolescents and young adults is available at NCCN.org/ patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Changes in fertility Treatment might cause your fertility to be temporarily or permanently impaired or interrupted. Hormonal birth control may or may not be recommended, so ask your doctor about options such as intrauterine devices (IUDs) and barrier methods. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding at the time of your cancer diagnosis, certain treatments will need to be avoided. Menstruation, menses, menstrual flow, or your “period” may stop during treatment, but often returns within 2 years after treatment in those 35 years of age and under. It is still possible to become pregnant even though you might not have a period. Therefore, birth control is recommended during and after treatment. Consult your doctor for the best time to plan a pregnancy. Those with testicles Cancer and cancer treatment can damage sperm. Therefore, use contraception (birth control) such as condoms to prevent pregnancy during and immediately after cancer treatment. Consider a zipper pocket to include a pen, small calendar, and insurance cards. Create folders for insurance forms, test types (ie, blood, imaging, pathology, radiology, genetics), treatments, and procedures. Organize items in the folder by date. Use online patient portals to view your test results and other records. Download or print the records to add to your binder. Add a section for questions and to take notes. Bring your medical binder to appointments. You never know when you might need it! Imaging tests Imaging tests take pictures of the inside of your body. Imaging tests show the primary tumor, or where the cancer started, and look for cancer in other parts of the body. A radiologist, an expert in interpreting imaging tests, will write a report and send this report to your health care provider (HCP). It is likely that the report will be sent directly to you through your patient portal or patient access system. You should discuss these results with your HCP. You will not have all of the following tests. Contrast material Contrast material is used to improve the pictures of the inside of the body. Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. It is used to make the pictures clearer. The contrast is not permanent and will leave your body in your urine immediately after the test. The types of contrast vary and are different for CT and MRI. Tell your care team if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys aren’t working well. CT scan A computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan uses x-rays and computer technology to take pictures of the inside of the body. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed picture. A CT scan of your head, neck, and chest, may be one of the tests to look for cancer. In most cases, contrast will be used. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use x-rays. Because of the very strong magnets used in the MRI machine, tell the technologist if you have any metal in your body. During the test, you will likely be asked to hold your breath for 10 to 20 seconds as the technician collects the images. Contrast is often used. A closed MRI has a capsule-like design where the magnet surrounds you. An open MRI has a magnetic top and bottom, which allows for an opening on each end. Closed MRIs are more common than open MRIs, so if you have claustrophobia (a dread or fear of enclosed spaces), be sure to talk to your care team about it. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and if they are using sugar produced by your body to grow. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. However, not all tumors will appear on a PET scan. Also, not all bright spots are cancer. It is normal for the brain, base of the tongue or tonsil lymphoid tissue, heart, kidneys, and bladder to be bright on PET. Inflammation or infection can also show up as a bright spot. When a PET scan is combined with CT, it is called a PET/CT scan. FDG-PET/CT An FDG-PET/CT uses a radiotracer called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG). It is made of fluoride and a simple form of sugar called glucose. You cannot eat or drink for at least 4 hours before the scan. This scan is most helpful when other imaging results are unclear. It may help find cancer in lymph nodes and distant sites. If it clearly shows cancer in the bone, a bone scan and sodium fluoride PET/ CT may not be needed. FDG-PET/CT can be done at the same time as a CT used for diagnosis. Ultrasound Ultrasound (US) uses high-energy sound waves to form pictures of the inside of the body. This is similar to the sonogram used for pregnancy. A wand-like probe (transducer) will be held and moved on your neck using gel. Ultrasound is painless and does not use x-rays, so it can be repeated as needed. Ultrasound is good at showing small areas of cancer that are near the skin. Sometimes, an ultrasound or CT is used to guide a biopsy. Panoramic dental x-ray A panoramic dental -ray or panoramic x-ray (Panorex) uses a very small dose of radiation to capture the entire mouth in one image, including the teeth, upper and lower jaws, and surrounding structures and tissues. A tracer is injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and if they are using sugar produced by your body to grow. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. However, not all tumors will appear on a PET scan. Also, not all bright spots are cancer. It is normal for the brain, heart, kidneys, and bladder to be bright on PET. Inflammation or infection can also show up as a bright spot. When a PET scan is combined with CT, it is called a PET/CT scan. lymph node (SLN) is the first lymph node that cancer cells are most likely to spread to from a primary tumor. Sometimes, there can be more than one sentinel lymph node. The lymph nodes removed are called the sentinel nodes. They may or may not contain any cancer cells. Just because these nodes are removed, it does not mean that they are positive for cancer. To find the sentinel lymph nodes, a radioactive material and other dyes are injected into the area where breast tumor is located. From here, the dye travels through the lymphatics in the breast to the lymph nodes. This helps the surgeon find which of the nodes are the sentinel lymph nodes. Skin biopsy A sample of inflamed skin on the breast will likely be removed to diagnose inflammatory breast cancer. Biopsy results Histology is the study of the anatomy (structure) of cells, tissues, and organs under a microscope. It is used to make treatment decisions. Your pathology report will contain information about histology. You may be recommended to have an open biopsy (surgery) to remove (excise) the tumor to confirm histology. Talk to your health care provider for more information on next steps. Hormone receptor status A hormone is a substance made by a gland in your body. Your blood carries hormones throughout your body. A receptor is a protein found inside or on the surface of a cell. Substances such as hormones attach (bind) to these receptors. This causes changes within the cell. Hormones recognize and bind to specific hormone receptors. When hormones attach to receptors on breast cancer cells, they can cause cancer to grow. If found, these receptors may be targeted using endocrine therapy. There are 2 types of hormone receptors: Estrogen – plays a role in breast development Progesterone – plays a role in menstrual cycle and pregnancy Hormone receptor (HR) testing should be done on any new tumors. A biopsy sample will be used. Hormone receptor-positive In hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, IHC finds estrogen and/or progesterone hormone receptors. Most breast cancers are . Estrogen receptor (ER) is stimulated by estrogen and provides survival and proliferation (rapid growth) signals. Cancer cells deprived of estrogen or which have their ER signal blocked with treatment may stop growing or die. Progesterone receptor (PR) binds progesterone and also provides survival and proliferation signals. It is thought that PR expression also suggests the tumor is estrogen dependent. breast cancer is treated with endocrine therapy, which blocks estrogen receptor signaling. Hormone receptor-negative Hormone receptor-negative (HR-) breast cancer cells do not have either estrogen or progesterone hormone receptors. These cancers are sometimes simply called hormone negative. HR- cancers often grow faster than cancers. Both the estrogen and progesterone receptors need to be negative for the cancer to be considered HR-. Estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer cells In breast cancer, testing finds estrogen hormone receptors in at least 1 out of every 100 cancer cells. In ER-low–positive invasive breast cancer, testing finds estrogen hormone receptors in 1 to 10 out of every 100 cancer cells. Endocrine therapy might not be recommended for ER-low–positive invasive breast cancer. HER2 status Inflammatory breast cancers often produce greater than normal amounts of HERHuman epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a protein involved in normal cell growth. It is found on the surface of all cells. When amounts are high, it causes cells to grow and divide. Some breast cancers have too many HER2 genes or receptors. Too many HER2s is called HER2-positive . You might hear it called HER2 overexpression or amplification. There are 2 tests for HER2: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) measures receptors. If the IHC score is , the cancer is . If the score is 0 or 1, it is considered HER2-. If the score is , further testing is needed. In situ hybridization (ISH) counts the number of copies of the HER2 gene. This test is done mainly when the IHC score is unclear. HER2 testing should be done on all new tumors. A tumor biopsy sample will be used. You might have more than one HER2 test. Immunohistochemistry Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is a special staining process that involves adding a chemical marker to cells. These cells are then studied using a microscope. IHC can find estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors in breast cancer cells. A pathologist will measure how many cells have estrogen and/ or progesterone receptors and the number of receptors inside each cell. Biomarker testing A sample from a biopsy of your tumor may be tested to look for specific DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) mutations/alterations, protein levels, or other molecular features. This information is used to choose the best treatment for you. It is sometimes called molecular testing or tumor profiling, tumor sequencing, gene expression profiling, or genomic testing. Biomarker testing includes tests of genes or their products (proteins). It identifies the presence or absence of mutations and certain proteins that might suggest treatment. Proteins are written like this: BRCA. Genes are written with italics like this: BRCA. HER2 and hormone receptor status are part of biomarker testing. Your treatment team will recommend the best types of biomarker testing that are important for you. Tumor markers Your blood or biopsy tissue may be tested for proteins

Antacids, heart or blood pressure medicine, and antidepressants are just some of the medicines that might interact with a systemic therapy. Therefore, it is very important to tell your care team about any medicines, vitamins, over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, herbals, or supplements you are taking. Bring a list with you to every visit. Chemoradiation is recommended for most locally advanced cervical cancers. These cancers have grown beyond the cervix but have not spread to the liver, lungs, or bones. See page 37 for more information on chemotherapy. Brachytherapy Also known as internal radiation therapy, brachytherapy involves treatment with radioactive material placed inside the body. Brachytherapy allows a high dose of radiation to be targeted at the tumor while limiting the amount delivered to surrounding normal tissue. During brachytherapy, instruments are placed into the cervix, uterus, and vagina. A radioactive material then travels into the instruments that have been placed in the body. This method is known as intracavitary brachytherapy. Sometimes, additional instruments (catheters, or thin hollow tubes) are placed in the tumor itself or in tissues next to the tumor (interstitial brachytherapy). For the treatment of cervical cancer, intracavitary brachytherapy is most often used. Interstitial brachytherapy is a specialized technique that is used for more advanced cancers that involve the parametrium. It is best performed at cancer centers with experience in this method. Brachytherapy for cervical cancer may be given in short bursts, called high dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy, or in long bursts, called low dose-rate (LDR) brachytherapy. Most centers currently use HDR brachytherapy. Treatment is typically given in 3 to 5 sessions over 2 weeks. If you have not had a hysterectomy, a device called an applicator is inserted into the uterus through the vagina. A “tandem and ring” applicator is commonly used for HDR brachytherapy. The tandem is a long, thin tube that extends into the uterus. The ring is a hollow circle that stays in the vagina, pressed against the cervix. A tandem and ovoid applicator uses hollow, rounded capsules instead of a ring. General anesthesia or deep sedation is often required, especially for the first applicator placement. The applicator is placed to align with the tissue targeted for treatment. Often, an imaging technique (MRI or CT) is used to guide placement of the applicator. These images are used to design the brachytherapy treatment plan. The applicator is connected to a brachytherapy machine. A radiation source travels from the machine through the hollow tubes and into the applicator. Treatment takes about 10 minutes. Sometimes brachytherapy is given as treatments over a couple days. In this case, the instruments are placed and left in the body until all the treatments have been given (1 to 2 days). You will need to remain in bed until treatment is complete so that the instruments don’t move. Brachytherapy is typically started in the final week or right after completing EBRT. Shrinking the tumor with EBRT first allows for better placement of the brachytherapy applicators. Treatment with both types of radiation therapy can be completed within 7 to 8 weeks. Chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy are types of systemic therapy. Most systemic therapies are given intravenously. This means they are slowly infused into your bloodstream through a vein. Infusions are often given in cycles of treatment days followed by days of rest. This allows your body to recover between cycles. Chemotherapy Platinum-based chemotherapy is the most commonly used systemic therapy for cervical cancer. It stops the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells or by stopping them from dividing. Cisplatin is generally preferred for platinumbased chemotherapy. If cisplatin is expected to be too harsh or cannot be given for other reasons, a different platinum drug called carboplatin may be used instead. As part of treatment with chemoradiation, cisplatin is typically given on a 7-day cycle (once weekly) for 5 to 6 weeks. Unlike chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy are most effective at treating cancers with specific features, called biomarkers. The side effects of chemotherapy depend on many factors, including the drug(s), the dose, and the person. In general, side effects are caused by the death of fast-growing cells, which are found in the intestines, mouth, and blood. of cervical cancer and for small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Physical exams Physical exams performed by your oncologist are an important part of surveillance, especially in the first 5 years after treatment. At these follow-up visits, tell your doctor about any changes in your health. Such changes include new or worsening symptoms and other health conditions or concerns. The recommended time frames for these follow-up visits are as follows: Years 1 and 2: Every 3 to 6 months Years 3, 4, and 5: Every 6 to 12 months After year 5: Once a year or as agreed upon with your doctor Time frame ranges are used to allow for differences in individual risk of recurrence and in patient and provider preference. Those considered at higher risk of recurrence may benefit from more frequent exams than those with a lower risk. After the fifth year, visits are generally spaced out to once per year. After fertility-sparing treatment, you may have an MRI of your pelvis (with contrast) 6 months after surgery and then yearly for 2 to 3 years. The area from the neck to the mid-thigh will be scanned. Other imaging for these stages may include a pelvic MRI with contrast 3 to 6 months after finishing treatment. Metastatic cancer For stage 4B or distant recurrences of cervical cancer, imaging is used mainly to learn how the cancer is responding to systemic therapy. Imaging may include CT, MRI, and/or PET/CT. Pap tests Depending on the type of surgery you have (if any), you may have annual Pap screening tests after treatment. Pap testing is helpful for finding new areas of abnormal and/or precancerous cells. It is not as good at detecting recurrent cervical cancer. Pap testing is also known as cervical or vaginal cytology. Blood tests If you have symptoms, or a physical exam was suspicious for recurrence, your doctor may order blood tests. In addition to a complete blood count (CBC), testing may measure blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels. These check your kidney function. Liver function tests may also be ordered. Survivorship In addition to surveillance testing, a range of other care is important for cancer survivors. This includes keeping alert for symptoms of cancer recurrence. See Part 6: Survivorship for more information. Recurrence This section discusses cervical cancer that does not improve with treatment (persistent) or that returns after treatment (recurrent). If your doctor suspects recurrence based on your symptoms or a physical exam, you will have imaging tests to check. This could include CT, PET, and/or MRI. Surgery to look inside the body (exploratory surgery) may be helpful in some cases. The goal is to learn the extent of the cancer. This can help guide treatment decisions. Biomarker testing Biomarkers are features of a cancer that can help guide treatment. Biomarkers are often mutations (changes) in particular genes. They can also be proteins that are made in response to the cancer. Biomarker testing is recommended for all recurrent cervical cancers. The results help determine whether treatment with certain targeted therapies is an option. The results can also be used to determine whether you can join certain clinical trials. Some doctors order biomarker testing early in the course of treatment. Many doctors wait and order it only if the cancer returns or spreads. Testing should be performed on tumor tissue removed during a biopsy or surgery when possible. Otherwise, a sample of blood may be tested instead. Other names for this testing include molecular testing, tumor profiling, genomic testing, tumor gene testing, nextgeneration sequencing (NGS), mutation testing, and comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP). Testing for PD-L1 expression is recommended for everyone with recurrent, progressive, or metastatic cervical cancer. If the PD-L1 level exceeds a set cutoff point, the cancer is considered PD-L1-positive. If needed, treatment with certain targeted therapies or immunotherapies may be an option for PD-L1–positive tumors. ---Role---

---Instructions---
1. **Entity Extraction:**
  - **Identification:** Identify clearly defined and meaningful entities only in the current user prompt's fenced `---Input Text---` section.
  - **Entity Details:** For each identified entity, extract the following information:
    - `name`: The name of the entity. If the entity name is case-insensitive, capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case). Ensure **consistent naming** across the entire extraction process.
    - `type`: Categorize the entity using the type guidance provided in the `---Entity Types---` section below. If none of the provided entity types apply, classify it as `Other`.

  - **Identification:** Identify direct, clearly stated, and meaningful relationships between previously extracted entities.
  - **N-ary Relationship Decomposition:** If a single statement describes a relationship involving more than two entities (an N-ary relationship), decompose it into multiple binary (two-entity) relationship pairs for separate description.

    - `target`: The name of the target entity. Ensure **consistent naming** with entity extraction. Capitalize the first letter of each significant word (title case) if the name is case-insensitive.
    - `keywords`: One or more high-level keywords summarizing the overarching nature, concepts, or themes of the relationship, separated by commas.
    - `description`: A concise explanation of the nature of the relationship between the source and target entities, providing a clear rationale for their connection.

3. **Relationship Direction & Duplication:**
  - Treat all relationships as **undirected** unless explicitly stated otherwise. Swapping the source and target entities for an undirected relationship does not constitute a new relationship.
  - Avoid outputting duplicate relationships.

4. **Output Limits & Prioritization:**
  - Output at most 100 total records across `entities` and `relationships` in this response.
  - Output at most 40 entity objects in this response.
  - Output fewer records if fewer high-value items are present. Do not try to fill the limit.
  - Only output relationship objects whose `source` and `target` are both included in the selected `entities` list for this response.
  - Within the list of relationships, prioritize and output those relationships that are **most significant** to the core meaning of the input text first.

Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is the molecule that carries genetic information in cells, serving as the fundamental blueprint for how cells grow, develop, and function. DNA is tightly packaged into chromosomes within the cell, and this genetic material is responsible for heredity and the regulation of cellular processes. Damage to DNA can cause cells to become abnormal, potentially leading to disease. Additionally, mutations in DNA can be identified through biomarker testing, and various diagnostic tests analyze DNA to detect such genetic alterations.

DNA is also the substrate for key molecular biology techniques: it is the genetic material that is sequenced by next-generation sequencing and amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). As the carrier of genetic information, DNA is central to understanding biology, genetics, and disease mechanisms.

Surgery is a broad medical term for procedures that involve physical intervention, typically through an incision, to treat disease, remove cancer or other tissue, or repair the body. In prostate cancer, surgery involves removing the cancerous tissue, which may include the tumor or the entire prostate, and is an option even for advanced stages. Surgery is also a key treatment for several other malignancies. Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Systemic Therapy is a broad category of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to reach and affect cancer cells throughout the body, rather than targeting a single localized area. These therapies are typically administered intravenously or orally, allowing the medicine to travel through the bloodstream to reach cells in any part of the body. This approach is used to treat various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), Ewing sarcoma, metastatic cervical cancer, and bladder cancer, among others. Systemic therapy can be employed as a primary treatment, as an initial therapy, or before or after surgery (neoadjuvant or adjuvant settings), and may also be used as maintenance therapy to prevent recurrence.

The main types of systemic therapy include chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. Chemotherapy uses drugs to kill rapidly dividing cancer cells, while targeted therapy focuses on specific molecules involved in cancer growth, such as HER2-targeted agents or inhibitors. Immunotherapy harnesses the body’s immune system to fight cancer. Other forms include endocrine (hormonal) therapy, which is often used in hormone-sensitive cancers, and platinum-based chemotherapy regimens. These treatments can be used alone or in combination, depending on the cancer type and stage.

Because systemic therapy affects cells throughout the body, it can impact both cancer cells and normal cells, leading to a range of potential side effects. Common short-term side effects include tiredness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, hair loss, mouth sores, loss of appetite, and low blood cell counts. Some side effects may be delayed and occur years after treatment. Additionally, certain systemic therapies, particularly some targeted treatments, can affect fertility. The specific side effects and their severity vary based on the drugs used, the dosage, and the individual patient.

In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. Therefore, while the scan is a powerful tool for detecting potentially cancerous cells, not all bright spots are malignant. To improve diagnostic accuracy and provide anatomical context, a PET scan is frequently combined with other imaging modalities, most commonly computed tomography (CT) in a PET/CT scan, or sometimes with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This combination allows for the precise localization of the metabolic hotspots identified by the PET scan, which is particularly valuable for cancer staging, treatment planning, and monitoring disease progression.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.

Targeted Therapy is a form of systemic cancer treatment that uses medicines or drugs to identify and attack specific molecules, genes, proteins, or receptors involved in the growth, spread, and survival of cancer cells. As a systemic therapy, it is generally reserved for cases where specific genetic targets are identified, and it may be employed when other treatments have failed or are unsuitable. The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

They are primarily responsible for defending the body against infectious diseases and foreign germs. These cells are derived from blood stem cells and are found circulating in the bloodstream as well as within the lymphatic system, where they act as infection-fighting cells in the lymph.

White blood cells are categorized into several main types, including granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are a specific and vital subtype of white blood cell. Because of their role in immunity, the antigens present on white blood cells serve as important biomarkers. Their concentration in the blood is a key health indicator, commonly measured as part of a Complete Blood Count (CBC) test.

The behavior and counts of white blood cells are clinically significant in various diseases. For instance, Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) originates in these cells, specifically in lymphocytes. Platelets, also known as thrombocytes, are small, non-nucleated cell fragments derived from blood stem cells (specifically megakaryocytes) that circulate in the blood. Their primary function is to control and prevent bleeding by adhering to damaged blood vessel walls and aggregating to form blood clots, a process essential for hemostasis and wound healing. By clumping together, they create a physical plug that stops or prevents hemorrhage, thereby helping to control bleeding.

Platelets are a critical component of the blood, and their quantity is routinely measured as part of a complete blood count (CBC). Their levels can be affected by various medical conditions and treatments; for instance, targeted therapies may reduce platelet counts, increasing the risk of bruising and bleeding. Additionally, low platelet counts are commonly observed in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). While often referred to as blood cells, they are technically cell fragments, and their role in clotting is vital for both normal wound repair and the prevention of excessive blood loss.

Bone marrow is the soft, sponge-like tissue located in the center of most bones, where blood cells are produced from blood-forming stem cells. It contains blood vessels and exists in two primary types: red marrow, which is active in blood cell formation, and yellow marrow, which is primarily fatty. As a key component of the lymphatic system, bone marrow is responsible for generating all types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, as well as B cells, which are crucial for immune function.

Bone marrow is clinically significant as the site of origin for several hematologic malignancies. In acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the bone marrow produces an excess of immature lymphocytes, while in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), it accumulates abnormal blasts. It is also the tissue where chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)-associated changes occur and where tumors such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) can be found. Additionally, bone marrow is the primary site where leukemia originates, making it a critical target for diagnosis and treatment.

Diagnostically, bone marrow samples are essential for karyotype analysis, as this procedure requires actively growing cells that are typically obtained from marrow or blood. In the context of cancer treatment, bone marrow can be damaged by the disease itself or by therapies such as chemotherapy or radiation. It is also the target of stem cell rescue procedures, where healthy blood-forming stem cells are harvested from the marrow, and it serves as the site where new cells grow following a transplant. Biopsies of bone marrow are commonly performed to confirm diagnoses such as follicular lymphoma (FL) and to assess disease involvement in various blood cancers.

The scope of biomarker testing is broad, encompassing various cancer types and specific markers. For instance, it is used to guide diagnosis and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and to assess risk and aggressiveness in prostate cancer by examining molecular components of biopsy samples. Common biomarkers tested include hormone receptors, HER2, PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, RET, p16, and EBV DNA, among others. These tests help determine the presence of specific biological markers that can predict response to particular drugs, thereby fine-tuning treatment plans and improving diagnostic accuracy.

Biomarker testing can be performed on tumor tissue or through liquid biopsies of blood, depending on the clinical need. The results provide critical information on the molecular profile of the cancer, enabling healthcare providers to select the most appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach. By identifying actionable mutations or protein levels, this testing plays a central role in precision medicine, ensuring that patients receive treatments most likely to be effective while avoiding unnecessary interventions.

FDG-PET/CT is a combined positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) imaging modality that utilizes the radiotracer fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), specifically the F-18 labeled form, to detect and assess metabolic activity in the body. This imaging test is primarily used in oncology to identify cancerous lesions, as malignant cells typically exhibit increased glucose uptake and metabolism, which the FDG tracer highlights. The integration of PET and CT allows for the precise localization of abnormal metabolic activity within the anatomical context provided by the CT scan.

This diagnostic tool is particularly valuable in the evaluation of suspected extramedullary leukemia, which refers to leukemic infiltration occurring outside the blood and bone marrow. In such clinical scenarios, FDG-PET/CT is employed when other imaging results are inconclusive or when there is a need to confirm the presence and extent of disease outside the primary hematopoietic sites. The scan is also broadly useful for detecting cancer activity in various other contexts, aiding in diagnosis, staging, and treatment planning.

A key procedural requirement for FDG-PET/CT is that the patient must fast for at least four hours prior to the scan. This fasting period is essential to ensure optimal tracer uptake by malignant tissues while minimizing interference from normal glucose metabolism, thereby enhancing the accuracy and clarity of the imaging results. Overall, FDG-PET/CT serves as a powerful and specific diagnostic tool, particularly when standard imaging methods are insufficient or when a high degree of metabolic detail is required.

Fertility preservation refers to the range of actions, methods, and processes undertaken to safeguard a person’s ability to have biological children in the future, most commonly discussed and implemented before cancer treatment that may impair fertility. This practice is centered on keeping reproductive options open for later in life, particularly for patients who are at risk of infertility due to medical interventions such as chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. The core objective is to protect or save eggs, sperm, or reproductive tissue so that individuals can potentially conceive biological children after their treatment concludes.

The specific techniques involved in fertility preservation include the collection and freezing of sperm or eggs, as well as more advanced procedures such as ovarian tissue banking and ovarian transposition. These methods are designed to enable future pregnancy by preserving reproductive cells or tissues prior to the start of cancer therapy. The process is typically discussed with patients before they begin treatment, ensuring that they are informed of their options and can make proactive decisions about their reproductive health. While the primary context is cancer care, the underlying principle of fertility preservation is broadly applicable to anyone seeking to maintain the possibility of having children later in life, whether due to medical reasons or personal choice.

default:summary:be53e874b99e7e395973ac01.return:
Ovaries are female reproductive organs located in the pelvis, typically grape-sized, that play a central role in sexual reproduction and endocrine function. They produce eggs (oocytes) necessary for fertilization and release key hormones, including estrogen and progesterone, which regulate the menstrual cycle and support secondary sexual characteristics. These organs are integral to the female reproductive system and are the primary site where ovarian cancer originates; their size, shape, and position are routinely assessed during a pelvic exam.

Ovaries are significantly impacted by cancer treatments. Radiation therapy can damage them, potentially leading to infertility, while chemotherapy and other treatments may also affect their function, impairing both fertility and hormone production. In surgical contexts, ovaries may be removed during procedures such as ovarian cancer surgery, pelvic exenteration, or radical cystectomy if cancer has spread. During a hysterectomy, ovaries may be either removed or left in place; their removal induces surgical menopause due to the sudden loss of hormone production. Additionally, women with Lynch syndrome have an elevated risk of developing cancer in the ovaries. Overall, the ovaries are vital for reproduction and hormonal balance, and their health is a key consideration in cancer treatment planning and surgical decision-making.

Claustrophobia is a dread or fear of enclosed spaces, a condition that holds particular relevance in the context of medical imaging, specifically regarding Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). This phobia can significantly affect a patient's ability to undergo an MRI, particularly when using a closed MRI scanner, which features a narrow, tube-like structure. Consequently, claustrophobia is a key factor that may influence a patient's choice between a closed MRI and an open MRI, as the latter provides a less confining environment.

The presence of claustrophobia is a critical consideration for both patients and their care teams when planning an MRI. Because closed MRI machines are more common than open ones, patients who experience this fear are advised to proactively discuss their condition with their healthcare providers before the procedure. This discussion allows the care team to make necessary accommodations or recommend alternative imaging options to ensure the patient's comfort and successful completion of the scan.

default:summary:6f0bb073e8e37d4d5dafc690.return: The bladder is a hollow, balloonlike organ located in the pelvis that stores urine until it is released from the body. In adults, it can hold up to 2 cups of urine. It is part of the urinary tract, situated near the prostate in males and near the cervix in females. The bladder normally appears bright on PET scans and is involved in the excretion of contrast material used in imaging studies. It may be affected by radiation therapy, particularly when treating nearby pelvic structures, and can be invaded by advanced anal tumors (stage IIIB). The bladder is also a key site for cancer, with bladder cancer originating in its lining. It is examined during cystoscopy and imaging for signs of malignancy, and it may be removed during radical cystectomy for bladder cancer or as part of pelvic exenteration.

Bone Scan is a nuclear medicine imaging test that uses a radioactive tracer, or radiotracer, to detect bone abnormalities, with a primary focus on identifying whether cancer has spread (metastasized) to the bones. The procedure is typically performed when a patient presents with symptoms such as bone pain or when they are considered to be at high risk for bone metastasis. During the scan, the radiotracer is injected, and areas of bone damage or abnormal activity appear as bright spots on the resulting images, helping clinicians pinpoint the location and extent of any cancerous involvement.

The test is also used more broadly to detect other bone abnormalities beyond cancer spread, serving as a general diagnostic tool for skeletal issues. However, its necessity is context-dependent: a Bone Scan may be deemed unnecessary if an FDG-PET/CT scan has already clearly demonstrated the presence of cancer in the bone, as the PET/CT result would already provide the required diagnostic information. In some clinical settings, the Bone Scan can be replaced by a sodium fluoride PET-CT, which offers an alternative imaging approach for similar indications. Ultimately, the decision to perform a Bone Scan is guided by clinical judgment, often triggered by specific symptoms or a high likelihood of metastatic disease, ensuring that the test is used efficiently within the broader diagnostic pathway.

In the context of oncology, mutations are frequently associated with cancer progression, as they can cause cells to grow out of control and become malignant. Blood is a specialized bodily fluid and tissue that circulates throughout the body, playing essential roles in transporting oxygen and nutrients to cells while carrying away metabolic waste products. It is composed of plasma and formed elements, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Beyond transport, blood is integral to the immune system, defending against pathogens, and to hemostasis, preventing bleeding through clotting mechanisms. Blood also serves as a conduit for hormones, facilitating endocrine signaling, and can be a vehicle for the spread of cancer cells during metastasis, as seen in conditions like liver cancer.

In clinical and diagnostic contexts, blood is a versatile sample source. It is used for genetic testing, including mutation and predisposition testing, as well as tumor marker tests. For certain procedures, such as karyotyping, a blood sample (or bone marrow) is required because it provides living cells that can be cultured and grown. Blood is also a critical medium for monitoring hematologic malignancies; for instance, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), it may contain an accumulation of immature blasts, while in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the overproduction of lymphoblasts can crowd out normal blood cell production. Additionally, blood can harbor cancer cells or circulating tumor DNA, making it a key specimen for liquid biopsies. In therapeutic contexts, blood is a source for harvesting stem cells, which can be used in transplantation and regenerative treatments.
